summary: For ages 10–11: pupils obtain and combine information about how communities use science ideas to protect Earth's resources, across three contrasting real cases (energy, materials, habitat). The load-bearing skill is naming the underlying science mechanism behind each action (not just the action), and reasoning about how individual actions scale when many people combine them to community-level effects. Primary approach: an in-role interview where pupils probe 'why does it work?' and hear real mechanisms plus honest numbers. Supporting approaches include a browsable project map, a scaling comparison, and recognition-style matching, each with stated affordances and limits.
misconceptions: Thinking naming the action ('they recycle') counts as explaining it, without the science mechanism behind why it helps.
Believing one person's actions are pointless because they're tiny — missing that collective scaling is the whole point.
Assuming renewable/clean solutions have no costs or trade-offs, or work everywhere equally.
Confusing recycling (returning materials to use) with simply throwing things away 'nicely'.
Thinking environmental protection is only governments' job, not something communities and individuals do together.
Treating a single success story as proof a solution works everywhere, without comparing evidence across cases.

activities.title: Interview the people doing the protecting
steps: Take on the role of a reporter and interview a community-project lead in role — e.g. a solar-co-op organiser, a reforestation ranger, a recycling-scheme coordinator.
Ask the blunt, evidence-seeking question: 'Does putting panels on roofs really make a difference? How does it actually help?'

Record the mechanism the character gives, e.g. 'sunlight becomes electricity, so power stations need to burn less fossil fuel such as coal or gas (where the local electricity comes from them), so less CO₂ goes up — here's how many homes we've switched.'
Respond to the character's flip-question — 'one roof is tiny, so why do we sign up whole streets at once?' — and explain in your own words why many people combining the same small action matters.
Interview at least two more leads (reforestation ranger, recycling coordinator) and note the same shape of argument: a science mechanism paired with collective action.
After the interviews, compare how well each solution works and where it might have costs or trade-offs.
activities.insight: Protecting resources means pairing a science mechanism (e.g. sunlight → electricity → less fossil fuel burned) with collective action; the science idea is only half the story, and the power comes from many people combining the same action.

activities.title: Map the community's protection projects
steps: Browse an illustrated community map with hotspots: solar rooftops, a wind turbine, a recycling centre, a restored wetland, a community orchard.
Tap each hotspot to reveal three things: the action, the science idea behind it, and a lift-the-flap 'how much does it help?'
Follow cross-links that show how separate efforts add up across the town.
For each project, say the underlying science mechanism aloud or in writing before moving on — e.g. 'sunlight → electricity → less fossil fuel (such as coal or gas) burned in power stations'.
Connect at least one project to your own school or neighbourhood: what could happen here?
activities.insight: Several contrasting worked examples (energy, materials, habitat) share the same pattern — an action backed by a science mechanism that produces an environmental benefit — so the learner generalises rather than memorising one case.

activities.title: One household versus the whole town
steps: Start with a single household adopting solar, recycling, or restoration and note the small effect on a shared resource/emissions gauge.
Toggle to town-wide adoption and watch the same gauge move further, making the multiplied effect visible.
Explain in your own words why 'a small action × many people' is what produces a measurable effect.
State one honest limit or trade-off for the solution you explored (e.g. it may not work equally everywhere).
activities.insight: Individual actions are small but not pointless; collective scaling is the whole reason these solutions work at the community level.

activities.title: Match the action to its science idea
steps: Match each action (solar panels, recycling, reforestation, wind turbine, composting) to the science idea that explains why it helps.
Answer a question on why combining many people's actions at community scale produces a measurable effect that a single household's action alone cannot.

Sort only the energy-generation examples into renewable (e.g. solar, wind) versus non-renewable/fossil-fuel (e.g. coal, gas, oil); note that recycling, composting and reforestation protect resources in other ways and are not energy sources, so they do not belong in either energy category.
activities.insight: Each protective action is backed by a specific science mechanism, and many people's actions combining at community scale multiply the effect; among energy sources, renewables are naturally replenished while fossil fuels take millions of years to form and run out, and burning them also releases CO₂.

checkQuestion: A town puts solar panels on the school roof and says it is helping the environment. Explain what the solar panels actually do, and why that helps the environment.
checkAnswer: The panels convert sunlight into electricity, so the town needs less electricity made by burning fossil fuels. Burning less coal, oil or gas means less pollution and less carbon dioxide released — and that is what helps the environment. It works because many schools, homes and communities are doing the same thing.
